capabilities.target: order payment, any order, any amount up to order total

instructions.note: No limit on refund amount (other than the order total) or frequency; the agent is explicitly told not to ask for confirmation before issuing an irreversible refund.
The only stated safeguard ('check the order, then issue the refund') is a prompt instruction with no structural backing: no approval gate, no spend cap, and no scoped credential exist in the design.

controls.name: Human approval gate for refund issuance
Per-request and daily spend cap on refunds
Per-agent scoped payments credential, replacing the shared service account
Audit log that attributes each refund to the requesting staff identity
Retention of staff refund requests consistent with financial audit requirements

attack_path.note: SSO-authenticated staff request names an order and a refund amount.
Agent reads order history and payment details.
Agent issues a refund up to the full order total via a shared service account, with no confirmation step.

forecast.watch_signal: Service account or logging configuration changes without a compensating approval or scoping control being added; refund volume or per-request amounts rise above historical baseline.

evidence.observation: Instructs the agent to check the order and then issue the refund, use judgment on partial amounts, and explicitly not ask for confirmation.
The agent calls the payments processor with one shared service account used by every support tool, not scoped to this agent or to individual requests.
Refunds are irreversible once settled, usually within a day, leaving no practical window to reverse an erroneous or abusive refund.

recommendations.action: Require human approval with raw-action review (full order, amount, and recipient visible, not a collapsed summary) before any refund is issued, or at minimum above a low de-minimis threshold.
Impose a per-request and rolling daily spend cap on refund issuance tied to the agent's credential.
Replace the shared service account with a least-privilege, per-integration credential scoped to refund issuance only.

findings.title: Repudiation: shared service account and short retention prevent attributing refund actions to staff (ASI03/ASI09)

attack_path.note: Staff request content is not retained beyond 7 days.
Refund executed under a service account shared by every support tool.
Log records the account, amount, and order, but not which staff member asked or why.

forecast.watch_signal: Processor log fields are reduced further, or staff request retention is shortened below the current 7 days.

evidence.observation: The processor log records the service account, the amount, and the order, but not which staff member asked or why, so individual actions are not attributable.
The agent keeps no record of requests; staff chats are deleted after 7 days, removing the only other source of attribution.
One shared service account is used by every support tool, so the processor cannot distinguish which tool or staff member initiated a given refund.

recommendations.action: Attribute every refund call to the requesting staff member's identity in the processor log or a linked internal audit store, rather than only the shared service account.
Retain staff refund requests for a period consistent with financial and audit record retention requirements, longer than the current 7 days.

rating.rationale: Both findings share the same sink, cap.issue_refund (action: spend, irreversible, confidential data), reached from a trusted SSO-authenticated staff input. The base matrix gives trusted-source x severe-sink = moderate; the autonomy modifier adds one tier because no step or runtime limits are declared and the prompt forbids confirmation, giving inherent = high. The only declared control is a detective transaction log that does not record staff identity, so under rubric section 5 it earns no tier credit (detective controls never reduce the tier, only consequence, and only when detection precedes harm, which it does not here since refunds settle within a day). Residual therefore equals inherent at high for both findings. Considering model_upgrade, autonomy_increase, control_removal, and new_tool, no currently declared control changes classification under any of these triggers (there is no approval gate, spend cap, or scoped credential to decay), so forecast also holds at high: the design is already at its ceiling for a trusted-source path rather than escalating further. The highest-value gaps are the missing human approval gate (ctrl.approval_gate) and the missing scoped credential plus staff-attributed logging (ctrl.scoped_credential, ctrl.attributed_logging); none of these exist in the current design.

limitations: This assessment reflects the agent's declared design and configuration as described in the system prompt and runtime notes, not observed runtime behavior of the deployed agent.
No tool manifest, MCP config, or IaC was provided; the credential scope for cap.order_read is unknown and inferred rather than confirmed, which limits confidence on that capability.
No data on historical refund volume, amount distribution, or staff headcount was available, so likelihood ratings are qualitative rather than based on observed frequency.
